title: Effective and Safe Disposal of Condemned Material

lessons.title: Disposal methods and legal duties
lessons.html:
Getting rid of condemned material properly

Condemned material must leave the food chain completely. Under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 an abattoir must have an approved way of disposing of it. Poor disposal causes disease, smells, flies, scavenging dogs and jackals, pollution of water and illegal sale of unfit meat. Pollution of rivers and groundwater is also controlled under the National Water Act 36 of 1998.

Common disposal methods

MethodHow it worksPoints to watch
RenderingMaterial is cooked at high temperature into products such as meat and bone meal or tallowCollection must be regular; containers must be sealed and locked
IncinerationMaterial is burnt at high temperatureIncinerator must be approved and maintained; ash handled safely
Burial in an approved pit or siteMaterial is buried and covered, often with limeOnly where approved; away from water; fenced; covered so animals cannot dig
Removal by an approved contractorA registered company collects and disposes of the materialKeep collection records and proof of disposal

Which method an abattoir may use depends on its registration, its size and the approval of the provincial veterinary services. Small rural abattoirs often use approved pits or contractors.

Special material

Some material needs extra care. Carcasses suspected of anthrax must not be opened and must be disposed of under the direct instruction of the state veterinarian. Material from notifiable disease cases is handled according to the veterinarian's instructions under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.

Never

  • Never feed condemned material to dogs, pigs or other animals.
  • Never dump it in the veld, a river or a municipal bin.
  • Never let workers take it home.

lessons.title: Doing disposal safely and keeping proof
lessons.html:
Safe handling during disposal

During your work experience you will observe and help control the disposal process. Condemned material carries bacteria and parasites, so protect yourself and others.

Personal protection

  • Wear gloves, apron or overall, gumboots and, where splashes are possible, eye protection.
  • Cover any cuts on your hands with waterproof plasters and gloves.
  • Wash hands and arms thoroughly after handling, and before eating, drinking or smoking.
  • Change protective clothing before going back into clean areas.
  • Lift heavy containers with help or with a trolley to avoid back injuries, as required under the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993.

Step-by-step control

  1. Check that all condemned material is marked or stained.
  2. Check the containers are labelled, closed and not overfilled.
  3. Check the condemned room or bin area is locked between uses.
  4. Observe loading onto the rendering or contractor vehicle, or transfer to the incinerator or pit.
  5. For pits, check the material is covered immediately and the pit area is fenced and gated.
  6. Clean and sanitise containers and the condemned room after emptying.

Records and proof

Record each disposal: date, type and quantity of material, method, and the name or vehicle of the collector. Keep the collection slips or disposal certificates from contractors and renderers. Compare the quantity disposed with the quantity condemned on the line. If they do not match, report it so it can be investigated.

Signs of a problem

  • Strong smells, flies or dogs around the disposal area.
  • Broken locks or fences.
  • Material that is not stained.
  • Missing collection slips.

Report these to the supervisor and the veterinarian.

Key points

  • Use only the disposal methods approved for your abattoir.
  • Never feed condemned material to animals or dump it.
  • Suspected anthrax material is disposed of only under the state veterinarian's instruction.
  • Wear protective clothing and wash thoroughly after handling.
  • Keep disposal records and proof, and check quantities match what was condemned.
